newsitem.title: USA: NYS gets approval to use managed care for Medicaid.
newsitem.headline: NYS gets approval to use managed care for Medicaid.

text.p: New York State Governor George Pataki Tuesday said Washington approved his plan to shift 2.4 million Medicaid clients to managed care, in order to cut the costs of providing health care for the poor.
Pataki said Medicaid recipients would get better treatment from managed care companies than from traditional, fee-for-service providers.

"Managed care, with its emphasis on prevention and early diagnosis of health problems, will significantly improve the health of our most vulnerable citizens, and reduce the need for Medicaid beneficiaries to rely on hospital emergency rooms for routine medical care," he said, in prepared remarks.

The state, which will start requiring Medicaid patients to use managed care in early 1998, now has 660,000 clients participating through its voluntary program. The Pataki Administration plans to have all those who are eligible enrolled by December 2000.
The New York Times, in its Tuesday edition, said Pataki had wanted to require Medicaid clients to join managed care programs in two years, a shorter time-frame than was agreed.

It added that the state's Medicaid program costs about $24 billion a year, an expense split between Washington and Albany, with localities paying about half the state share. Twelve other states already have received permission from Washington for similar managed care programs, the Times said.
New York City, which the paper said has almost three-quarters of the state's Medicaid patients, immediately will start requiring them to join managed care networks.
Eight upstate counties will do so this summer: Albany, Columbia, Erie, Genesee, Greene, Niagara, Rennsalaer and Saratoga.

New York State for the first time will get matching federal funds to pay the health care costs of its 370,000 Home Relief recipients, mainly childless, able-bodied adults. The state and localities now pay for these costs as these individuals do not qualify for federal welfare aid and often are not eligible for Medicaid, the Times said.

Further, New York State will set up special plans for people with HIV infection or AIDs and those with serious mental illnesses. Until such plans are set up, these individuals will not have to use managed care.

Donna Shalala, the U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary, said, "The waiver contains strong protections for Medicaid's most vulnerable recipients, including adults and children with special needs, pregnant women, and people with HIV/AIDs. And we have worked to ensure that hospitals that provide care to our most vulnerable citizens can make a smooth transition to managed care."

New York State will set up a $1.25 billion fund, using $250 million a year, to help voluntary and public hospitals make the transition to a managed care system. Washington will provide new funds to help hospitals that care for a large ratio of Medicaid clients -- at least 20 percent -- and indigent, uninsured patients.

Pataki added that the mandatory managed care programs will have to adhere to consumer protections that became law in 1996, which set out a process for resolving complaints and require Albany to monitor quality with regular audits.
